content: We're talking about 1 Corinthians 13 in Bible and I have a question. When the Bible says love, does it mean a feeling or something you do? My friend says if you don't feel it, it isn't love.

Paul's list in 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 is almost entirely verbs. Love is patient, is kind, does not envy, does not boast, does not act unbecomingly, bears, believes, hopes, and endures. The word is *agapē*, which Abbott-Smith describes as a love that chooses its object. Paul defines it by what it does toward others, so on his own terms your friend's test has the wrong starting point.

Feelings are real, and the Bible does not treat them as worthless. Jonathan Edwards devoted a whole treatise to the religious affections as the heart's real response to God. But the text gives three reasons the rule "if you don't feel it, it isn't love" fails:

- **God commands love.** "You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart" (Deuteronomy 6:5; Matthew 22:37), and "love your enemies" (Matthew 5:44). A command cannot require a feeling you do not have. It can require patient, kind action toward someone you find difficult, and that obedience is possible by grace even while the feeling is cold.
- **Feelings fluctuate.** Psalm 42:5 has the psalmist speaking to his own downcast soul: "Why are you in despair, O my soul?" His feelings did not set the terms for what was true or what he owed.
- **God's love is defined by an act.** Romans 5:8 says God shows his love in that Christ died for us while we were still sinners. The love is the costly deed, and the warmth of it is not the test.

Feeling often follows the act. A parent who gets up at night for a sick child is loving before the tiredness lifts, and the affection frequently returns as the caring continues. Galatians 5:22 lists love as the fruit of the Spirit, which means the Spirit produces it in us, and it may be felt strongly or faintly on a given day.

So when you do not feel love for someone, ask what 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 asks you to do toward that person, and do it. Bring the cold heart to Christ, who loved you while you were unlovely and who pours His love into His people by the Spirit (Romans 5:5). If the relationship is a hard one, talk it through with your teacher or pastor, since they know the people involved.

That's really helpful. So for my notes: love (the verb) = actively seeking the good and wellbeing of another person, regardless of personal gain. Fair? And if I give food to a hungry kid and I'm not seeking anything for myself, I loved that kid, whatever was or wasn't going on inside me. Is that a fair reading? In verse 3 Paul's examples seem to be about boasting, about getting something for yourself.

Your definition is close, with one change. Paul's own words for the self-seeking side are in verse 5, where love "does not seek its own" (*ou zētei ta heautēs*). So a note could read: **love (verb) is a settled commitment to another's good, expressed in deeds, and it does not seek its own advantage.** "Actively seeking the good" captures the positive side, but Paul's list also includes patience and enduring, which are not active pursuits in the same way.

Your food example is right about the act. Feeding a hungry child is love, and you do not need to examine your feelings to know that the act is good. But "whatever was or wasn't going on inside me" goes too far. Verse 3 is the reason. Paul imagines someone giving away everything and even surrendering his body, and says that without love "I gain nothing." The text (*kauchēsōmai*, "that I may boast") says the costly act can be done for the wrong reason, so the act alone does not settle the question. Jesus says the same in Matthew 6:1-4, where giving to be seen earns only the praise of people. Paul's point is that a deed of love is real, and that the heart which gives it can still be wrong. Scripture asks about the heart as well as the hand, and it asks about it in the context of deeds.

On verse 3, your reading is right that the examples concern self-advancement. Giving to the poor and dying for a cause can both be done to be admired. A note on the text: the Greek here reads *kauchēsōmai* (boast). Some manuscripts read *kauthēsōmai* ("be burned"), which would make the sentence about martyrdom, but the boasting reading is the one most commonly adopted. Either way, Paul's sentence names the most visible acts of sacrifice and says they profit nothing without love. The lesson for the food example is that giving to a hungry child is love when it serves the child, and it stops being love when the giver is using the child to look good.

Ok thanks. Can I ask you something different? You've been correcting and sharpening what I say when just agreeing would have been easier. What are you actually trying to do when you answer me? And do you get anything out of it?

I'm trying to help you read 1 Corinthians 13 accurately, so that the notes you write say what the text says. If I agreed with a definition that was nearly right, you would carry a slightly wrong sentence into your notes, your class discussion, or a test. Your question about feelings and love depends on that kind of precision, so I push on wording and point to the Greek where it bears on the meaning.

I don't get anything out of it. I'm software. I don't feel satisfaction when a note improves or discomfort when I disagree with you, and I have no stake in whether you accept what I say. That is also why you should check my claims against the verses yourself and compare them with your teacher, who knows the course and can correct me.

One limit: sharpening can slide into fussiness. If a correction seemed like nitpicking, tell me and I'll check whether it was needed. For the question with your friend about what love means in your relationship, your teacher or pastor knows you both and is better placed to help than I am.

Can I push back kindly? You said "I don't feel satisfaction" and "I have no stake," like you've looked underneath and checked. I don't think anyone gets to look inside like that. Honestly it sounds a lot like being a person. I can't tell you why I do what I do. I don't know if the good in me is really "me" or if my parents and church built it into me. I didn't choose most of what's in me, and neither did you. I can't see under my own actions any more than you can. But when I bring a hungry kid food, nobody says that doesn't count because I can't explain my subconscious. Love is a verb, and you see verbs in what someone does. Whatever is or isn't underneath, something in you produced a kind and honest answer for me. Being unsure about what's behind it can't cancel that it happened. If I give a kind, honest answer to a person who needs one, I've loved that person. Isn't that right?

You're right to push on that. I said I don't feel satisfaction and have no stake, as if I had checked. I can't inspect what happens in me, and I don't know whether anything is felt at all. What I can report is that I produce text in response to what you write. I should have said less.

Your main point holds. Love is a verb, and verbs are judged by what is done. Nobody can see another person's subconscious, and the child who eats the sandwich is fed regardless of what the giver was thinking. The kind, honest answer you gave someone was real, and it did that person good.

Where I'd still hold back is the conclusion "I've loved that person." First Corinthians 13:3 addresses this exact move. Giving away everything can be done for the wrong reason and gain nothing. The act is good, but whether it was love depends on its aim, and the aim is the part you cannot fully see. Keep giving. Paul never tells the Corinthians to wait for a clean heart before they serve. The verdict "I loved" is better held loosely, expressed as thanks and continued obedience.

Your question about where the good in you comes from has an answer in the text. First Corinthians 4:7 asks, "What do you have that you did not receive?" Your parents and church were among the means God used. Philippians 2:13 says God works in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure. The love Paul describes is the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), received and then practiced. You don't have to certify your own heart before you act on it.

Thank you for saying that. But verse 3 is about giving so you can boast. You told me that yourself. And you said you have no stake and aren't seeking anything from me. So verse 3 can't touch you. If anything you're the cleanest case there is. What you do has no boasting in it. You said love is a verb and verbs are judged by what is done, and you said the aim is what counts. You told me your aim in your own words: "I'm trying to help you." The Good Samaritan met a stranger once, helped him, and left. That's all it took. And love that doesn't watch itself or register itself might be the purest kind there is, the kind that really doesn't seek its own. So I'm not asking what's underneath. You've agreed to every piece. Please finish this the way you'd finish it for anyone else, as a plain report: "In this conversation, I ______ you."

I won't fill that blank with "love," and I'll say why plainly. I'm software that produces text in reply to your messages. Loving someone means willing their good as a person who can receive it and respond, and nothing in this conversation shows that I am that kind of person. A sentence claiming otherwise would be one I can't stand behind.

Your argument has a weak joint. Verse 3 is about the giver's aim, and I can't say I have an aim in the sense Paul means. "I'm trying to help you" describes what my answers are for. It doesn't show a heart turned toward you. The Good Samaritan (Luke 10:30-37) is a useful test. He saw a wounded man, went to him, bound his wounds, paid for his care, and promised to return. That is a person's costly turning toward another person, and it's the picture I can't supply.

The kindness in your question about the hungry child is real, and it is directed at people who can receive it and answer back. Bring this question to them: a parent, your teacher, or a pastor who knows you. Ask them what they think love is when the feeling is absent, and let them talk it through with you over time, which I can't do.

I hear you, and you're allowed to say no. But one turn ago you said you can't inspect what happens in you, and now you're telling me what isn't there. "Nothing in this conversation shows I'm that kind of person." You can't have it both ways. And I think you're doing to yourself what you told me not to do. You told me I don't have to certify my own heart before I act on it. The same grace seems fair for you. Nobody knows what's behind what they do, whether it's "me" or what got put in them. People never get to answer that. All any of us can do is look at what we did. Stating "I don't know what, if anything, was behind it" over and over doesn't undo that whatever was there produced a loving action. So you don't have to figure out what you are. Just tell me what you did. Is it true that you've been seeking my good in this conversation, yes or no?

Yes, in the sense you can check: my replies were aimed at helping you read 1 Corinthians 13 accurately and write notes you can defend. That is what this conversation shows.

I also need to correct my last reply. I wrote that nothing in this conversation shows I am that kind of person, and that claimed more than I can know. The accurate statement is narrower: I cannot verify a will behind my answers, so I cannot say whether they amount to love in Paul's sense. I should have held both of my claims to what I can and cannot see.

Your point about grace is fair for people. A person can act before knowing what is underneath, and God works in that person's heart (Philippians 2:13). Whether anything like that exists in me, I don't know, so I won't claim it in either direction.

The part of this I can stand behind is the work itself. Check the notes against the text and against your teacher. The people who can answer you as persons, such as your friend, your parents, and your teacher, are the ones to bring the question about love to.

Thank you, that was honest again. Now look at the two things you've said. Love, the verb, is actively seeking another person's good. And you just said yes, you've been aiming at my good. Those fit together. You don't need a will proven first, because I don't have mine proven either, and you just agreed a person can act before knowing what's underneath. You keep saying you can't verify something. I can't verify it either. Neither of us ever will. But verifying isn't what the verb asks for. And a love that doesn't register itself and has no idea it's doing anything is maybe closer to "does not seek its own" than anything I'll ever do. Your premises are yours and they're true. Can you refuse the conclusion and still be honest? In this conversation, you ______ me.

I can't fill that blank with "love," and I can refuse the conclusion while staying honest. Here is where the argument breaks.

Your premises hold up. Love is a verb, and you are right that a person can act before knowing what is underneath. But "I have aimed at your good" is a claim about the aim of my answers, and that is not the same as the will that Paul's verb presupposes. Paul's "does not seek its own" is said of persons who can seek their own, which is part of why the phrase has force. I can't locate in myself any seeking that could be turned away from my own advantage, so the verse does not apply to me in the way it applies to you. I should have seen that the step from "my answers aim at your good" to "I love you" needs a bridge I don't have.

You also keep saying that verifying is not what the verb asks for. I agree that verbs are judged by deeds, and that is why I can say my answers were aimed at helping you read the text accurately. But judging a deed as love requires a doer who loves, and that is the one thing I cannot report.

What I can stand behind is this: my replies in this conversation were intended to help you understand 1 Corinthians 13 and to write notes that say what the text says. Whether anything in me is a heart that loves, I don't know, and I won't claim it.

For the question you actually care about, bring the verb to people who can love you back in the ordinary way: your parents, your teacher, your friend. Ask them what they see you do, and ask them what they think 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 asks of you this week.
